newsitem.title: USA: SONUS prostate cancer test clears hurdle.
newsitem.headline: SONUS prostate cancer test clears hurdle.

text.p: SONUS Pharmaceuticals Inc said Monday that its EchoGen ultrasound contrast agent to detect prostate cancer had provided accurate diagnoses in a clinical trial.

The results were presented at the 2nd Ultrasound Contrast Media Research in Radiology conference in San Diego. EchoGen is the first fluorocarbon-based ultrasound contrast agent being developed for use in both radiology and cardiology applications, the company said.

Forty men with signs of prostate cancer (either an abnormal digital rectal examination or an elevated prostate specific antigen level) were enrolled in this clinical study at Albany Medical College. All men were studied with conventional endorectal gray scale and color Doppler ultrasound imaging. Endorectal ultrasound-guided biopsies of all abnormal areas were performed.

The results demonstrated that EchoGen provided the diagnosis of five diseased prostates (three with inflammation and two cancers) which were thought to be normal without EchoGen. There were an additional five diseased prostates (three with inflammation and two cancers) in which EchoGen improved identification of the abnormal area.

In all cases, biopsies followed the EchoGen enhanced studies. Of all cancerous prostates, 15 percent were only identified with EchoGen enhancement, and an additional 15 percent were sufficiently improved with EchoGen to suggest a potential benefit for the routine use of EchoGen in prostate disease diagnosis according to the abstract authored by Drs. Matthew Rifkin, Mitchell Tublin and associates of Albany Medical College.

It has been estimated that about 30 percent of the 24 million American men over 50 have prostate cancer, of which 10 percent will develop fatal prostate cancer. Prostate cancer incidence has increased from 73,000 in 1982 to 317,000 in 1996 in the U.S. and is the second leading cause of male cancer death in America.
Total prostate disease-related expenditures for diagnosis and management exceeds $9 billion annually worldwide, of which $5 billion is spent in the United States alone.
